criterion_scores.reasoning: The guide is internally coherent and the major prescriptive sections line up: voice/tone, opener rules, CTA guidance, character budget, learn-more set, and visual workflow. I checked the whole document and did not find a behavioral contradiction. The only issue I found was an unsupported verification claim in the budget section, which is more of a diagnostics/honesty problem than a logic error.

All of the expected guide sections are present at useful depth: voice, audience, post architecture, data points, formatting, learn-more set, DM structure, quality bar, audience priority, positioning, and visuals. I looked for missing load-bearing sections or TODOs and did not find any. Minor nit: the document is very dense and somewhat repetitive, but not incomplete.

The file is in the expected `.claude/references/` location and uses the reference-doc style consistently. I did not see a naming or placement violation. I also checked for obvious house-context conflicts and found none. Minor nit: a few lines make implementation-sounding claims (e.g. about verification or imports) that are stronger than a pure reference guide usually needs.

The guide avoids the obvious anti-patterns called out in the rubric: it is not a bullet-lattice fallback, does not duplicate the Scan head, and does not introduce tombstoned tooling. I checked for gratuitous ceremony or speculative surface area and found little beyond the unavoidable breadth of a style guide. The only mild concern is some prescriptive over-specificity, but it is still mostly purposeful.

Most rules are legible and actionable, and the section structure is easy to navigate. However, the document occasionally overstates certainty, most clearly at line 98 with 'verified June 2026'. I also noticed other factual-sounding claims without explicit sourcing, so the honesty/verification discipline is not perfect.

defects.quote: **The LinkedIn feed-post hard cap is 3,000 characters** (stable since June 2023; verified June 2026).
defects.description: This states a fact as verified without any source or method in the document. It reads as an overclaim of certainty, which conflicts with the rubric's requirement to be honest about what is actually verified.
